B is a row of four squares with one square above and one below the right end. C is a row of four squares with one square above the right end and one below the left end. D is a row of four squares with two more squares stacked above the right end. E is a row of four squares with one square above and one below the second square. F is a block of two rows of three squares. G is a row of four squares with one square above each end. H is a row of four squares with one square above the right end and one below the second square. I is a cross-like shape made of a top square, a middle row of two squares, and one square below the right one.
figures.original: Which of these nets would make a closed cube?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Mathematics Stage 5 Learners Book
figures.shows: Nine blue rectangles of different sizes are scattered on a page, each labelled with a single capital letter from A to I. A is a large square-like rectangle, B is a medium wide rectangle, C is a long wide rectangle, D is a long wide rectangle, E is a small wide rectangle, F is a wide rectangle, G is a tall rectangle, H is a tall rectangle, and I is a small square. No measurements are printed.
figures.original: Which of these six rectangles can be put together to make the net of a cuboid?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Mathematics Stage 5 Learners Book

A smaller brown square sits above the green one, and a smaller dark blue square sits below the red one. On the right is a closed cuboid, long and horizontal, with a red front face, a yellow top face and a dark blue right end face.
figures.original: Does this net make the cuboid?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Mathematics Stage 5 Learners Book
figures.shows: Four drawings labelled A, B, C and D show arrangements of coloured cubes on a table, each seen from a different side. Each arrangement has a red cube with a yellow cube on top of it. In A, a blue cube with a purple cube behind it sits at the left, and a green cube and an orange cube sit at the right. In B, an orange cube is at the left, a green cube is behind, and a purple cube and a blue cube are in front at the right. figures.original: Below are four drawings of cubes on a table from different sides.Two of the pictures show Marie's arrangement but from different views. Which are the pictures of Marie's cubes?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Mathematics Stage 5 Learners Book

figures.original: (b) Copy and complete the Venn diagram.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Mathematics Stage 5 Learners Book

figures.original: Look at the middle row of triangles. Each triangle is translated right to make the pattern. How many centimetres is each triangle translated to the right?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Mathematics Stage 5 Learners Book

figures.original: How many equilateral triangles can you find in this diagram?

figures.original: Find a path through the grid to the bottom row. Start at a kite in the top row. You can move to a next door kite if it is a reflection of the kite you are on. The kite can be a reflection in a horizontal or vertical mirror line.

To the left of the line are a red vertical line in row 1, a green vertical line spanning rows 2 to 4, a blue vertical line spanning rows 3 to 5, an orange right-angled triangle in row 1 to 2 with its vertical side on the right, and a purple square 2 by 2 squares in the bottom left. Nothing has been reflected yet on the right side of the mirror line.
figures.original: Copy the coloured lines, shapes and mirror line onto square paper. Reflect each of the coloured lines and shapes in the mirror line.

A board headed "Postage Costs" lists: up to 1 kg $2.50, up to 2 kg $5.60, up to 10 kg $19.65, up to 25 kg $27.70.
figures.original:
(a) Put the parcels in order from lightest to heaviest.

figures.original: Estimate the size of each angle.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics Learners Book 7

figures.original: Calculate the values of a, b, c and d. Give reasons for your answers.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics Learners Book 7

figures.original: Copy the diagram and write in the size of all the other angles.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics Learners Book 7

figures.original: Work out the unknown angles a, b and c.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics Learners Book 7

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics Learners Book 7

figures.original: AB and CD are parallel lines. Calculate s and t.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics Learners Book 7

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics Learners Book 7

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics Learners Book 7

figures.original: The diagram shows angle X is 45°. a Calculate a.

Now I compare 1/4 and 3/10, using a common denominator of 40.
I compare 25/4 and 63/10, using a common denominator of 40.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge-IGCSE-Biology-MARRY-JONES-4th-Ed

E marks a vascular bundle, F points to a cell in the lower layer, and G and H point to parts near the bottom surface.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge-IGCSE-Biology-MARRY-JONES-4th-Ed
figures.shows: A line graph with carbon dioxide concentration on the x-axis and rate of photosynthesis on the y-axis. The x-axis is marked with the points A, B, C and D. The upper curve is labelled 'high light intensity' and the lower curve is labelled 'low light intensity'.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge-IGCSE-Biology-MARRY-JONES-4th-Ed

Distance moved by meniscus after 30 minutes / mm

figures.textbookName: Cambridge-IGCSE-Biology-MARRY-JONES-4th-Ed

The beaker holds some liquid, and a label on the base reads 'TRIAL 2'.
figures.original: Two students carried out an experiment to investigate the effect of carbon dioxide concentration on the rate of photosynthesis of an aquatic plant. The photograph shows some of the apparatus that they used.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge-IGCSE-Biology-MARRY-JONES-4th-Ed

figures.textbookName: Cambridge-IGCSE-Biology-MARRY-JONES-4th-Ed

Ten parts are marked with lines to the letters A to J: A at the mouth/tongue region, B at the tube running down the throat, C at the stomach, D at the structure beside the stomach, E at the tube below the stomach, F at the coiled small intestine, G at the large intestine, H at the lower end of the gut, I at the opening at the bottom, and J at the dotted liver on the left side of the figure. Three teeth are labelled with lines: A points to a front tooth at the centre of the arch, B points to a pointed tooth beside the front teeth, and C points to a large tooth at the back of the jaw.
figures.original: The diagram shows the teeth in the upper jaw of a human.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge-IGCSE-Biology-MARRY-JONES-4th-Ed
figures.shows: A black-and-white light micrograph of a section through two villi of the small intestine. figures.original: The photograph shows a section through two villi from the human digestive system.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge-IGCSE-Biology-MARRY-JONES-4th-Ed
figures.shows: A light micrograph of a transverse section through part of a leaf, stained blue-green so the cell walls show. In the centre is a vascular bundle with a semi-circle of empty xylem vessels with purple walls, and smaller cells lie below them. Large thin-walled cells with mostly empty spaces surround the bundle, and a layer of small cells forms the outer edge. The leaf blade extends to the upper right. There are no labels or printed values.
figures.original: Look at Figure 8.6. It shows part of a plant leaf, cut across. A stain has been used to colour the cell walls. The xylem vessels are the empty cells with purple walls, arranged in a semi-circle.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge-IGCSE-Biology-MARRY-JONES-4th-Ed
figures.shows: A coloured micrograph of a plant stem cut across, roughly circular with a wavy outline on a black background. The outer layer is bright green, and inside it is a thick band of yellow-brown cells. The centre is filled with green cells of varying sizes. Six blue patches containing large dark holes (xylem vessels) lie in a ring near the edge of the green central region. There are no labels or printed values.
figures.original: Look at Figure 8.4. It shows a plant stem, cut across. The xylem vessels have been coloured blue.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge-IGCSE-Biology-MARRY-JONES-4th-Ed

figures.original: Use your diagrams from Activity 8.1, and the diagrams in Figures 8.7, 8.8 and 6.11, to describe in words the positions of xylem and phloem in roots, stems and leaves.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge-IGCSE-Biology-MARRY-JONES-4th-Ed
figures.shows: A 3D drawing of a cylindrical slice of a plant stem (or root). Six vascular bundles are arranged in a ring just inside the epidermis, each with red xylem on the inside and blue phloem on the outside. Two bundles are pulled up out of the slice: a blue phloem column on the left and a red xylem column on the right. The green cortex fills the rest of the slice. Labels point to the phloem, vascular bundle, xylem, epidermis and cortex.
figures.original: Use your diagrams from Activity 8.1, and the diagrams in Figures 8.7, 8.8 and 6.11, to describe in words the positions of xylem and phloem in roots, stems and leaves.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge-IGCSE-Biology-MARRY-JONES-4th-Ed
figures.shows: A photograph of the cut end of a green celery stalk, seen from the side with the cut face at the top. The cut face is pale and curved in a U shape. Small orange-red coloured spots lie in a curved row near the outer edge of the cut face, following the U shape. The green stalk with vertical ridges is visible below the cut. There are no labels.
figures.original: From the position of the coloured areas in the stalk in Figure 8.14, and in your own celery stalk, which tissue in the stalk do you think contains the coloured water?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge-IGCSE-Biology-MARRY-JONES-4th-Ed
figures.shows: A line drawing of an upright plant stem with lobed, toothed leaves attached along it. Near the lower part of the stem a section has been removed as a ring. Label X points to the stem just above the gap, and label Y points to the stem just below the gap.
figures.original: The diagram shows a plant that has had a ring of tissue removed from its stem.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge-IGCSE-Biology-MARRY-JONES-4th-Ed
figures.shows: Three photographs side by side of the same potted plant with green leaves in a brown pot on a brown saucer. In the left photograph the plant is healthy, with leaves held out horizontally and spread widely. In the middle photograph the leaves and upper stems droop downward and the plant looks wilted. In the right photograph the leaves and stems droop even more and the plant is more collapsed.
figures.original: Look at the wilted plant in Figure 8.18. Suggest how wilting might help a plant to survive the shortage of water that has caused it to wilt.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge-IGCSE-Biology-MARRY-JONES-4th-Ed
figures.shows: A potometer: a leafy plant shoot is attached by tubing to a vertical capillary tube whose lower end stands in a beaker of water. A ruler marked 0 to 15 cm is placed beside the capillary tube. The tube contains water and an air bubble near the bottom, close to the 1 cm mark on the ruler.
figures.original: A student set up the apparatus shown in the diagram.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge-IGCSE-Biology-MARRY-JONES-4th-Ed
figures.shows: A table with three columns: Time / minutes, and Position of air bubble / mm split into 'No fan' and 'With fan'. Rows: 0 min: 8 (no fan), 10 (with fan); 2 min: 11, 14; 4 min: 15, 19; 6 min: 18, 24; 8 min: 21, 29; 10 min: 25, 34.
figures.original: The table shows her results.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge-IGCSE-Biology-MARRY-JONES-4th-Ed
figures.shows: Two circular transverse-section diagrams side by side. The left one, labelled 'root', is a large circle with a small central region in which a five-pointed star-shaped tissue is labelled X. The right one, labelled 'stem', is a large circle with eight oval vascular bundles arranged in a ring near the edge. Four labels, A, B, C and D, point to one bundle on the right: A points to the outer edge of the stem, B to the outer part of the bundle, C to the inner part of the bundle, and D to the tissue between the bundles.
figures.original: The diagrams show a transverse section through a root and a stem. Which label on the diagram of the stem indicates the same tissue as X?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge-IGCSE-Biology-MARRY-JONES-4th-Ed
figures.shows: Four leaves labelled P, Q, R and S hang from a horizontal string. P has its upper surface covered with petroleum jelly, Q has its lower surface covered with petroleum jelly, R has both surfaces covered with petroleum jelly, and S has no petroleum jelly.
labels: upper surface covered with petroleum jelly
lower surface covered with petroleum jelly
both surfaces covered with petroleum jelly
figures.original: The diagram shows an experiment set up by a learner.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge-IGCSE-Biology-MARRY-JONES-4th-Ed

Three labels X, Y and Z have lines pointing to: X a large outer cell, Y a small-celled region between the arms, and Z a large wide cell in the central cluster.

figures.original: Leaves lose water vapour through their stomata. The micrograph shows a surface view of the lower epidermis of a leaf.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge-IGCSE-Biology-MARRY-JONES-4th-Ed

figures.original: Look at the ECG in Figure 9.9.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge-IGCSE-Biology-MARRY-JONES-4th-Ed
figures.shows: A vertical section through a mammalian heart, drawn in outline with the four chambers and the major vessels. Four chambers are labelled with lines: S is the upper chamber on the left side of the page, P is the upper chamber on the right side of the page, R is the lower chamber on the left side of the page, and Q is the lower chamber on the right side of the page. Valves are drawn between the upper and lower chambers, and vessels enter and leave at the top.
figures.original: The diagram shows a section through the heart. Which two areas contain deoxygenated blood?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge-IGCSE-Biology-MARRY-JONES-4th-Ed
figures.shows: A simplified diagram of blood vessels supplying abdominal organs. A long vessel on the right, labelled F, has arrows pointing downwards. A long vessel on the left has arrows pointing upwards and is labelled G at its lower end. Branches from the right vessel lead to the liver, the gut and the kidney, and return to the left vessel. A vessel labelled H runs from the gut to the liver. The kidney is joined to both the right and left vessels.
figures.original: The diagram shows some of the blood vessels supplying organs in the abdomen. What are blood vessels F, G and H?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge-IGCSE-Biology-MARRY-JONES-4th-Ed
figures.shows: A line graph of the volume of the left ventricle (y-axis, no numerical values) against time in seconds (x-axis, 0 to 1.2 in steps of 0.1). The volume rises to a plateau at about 0.1 s, then falls steeply after point A (about 0.18 s) to a minimum at point B (about 0.45 s). It then rises, with a small step at about 0.75–0.8 s, to a peak near 0.85 s, and falls again to a low level by about 1.1–1.2 s.
figures.original: The graph below shows how the volume of the left ventricle changes over a time period of 1.2 seconds.

Label A points to the dark nucleus region at the top right, B points to a small structure in the wall at the bottom, and C points to the gap (white space) between the red blood cell and the wall on the right. The red blood cell is labelled.
figures.original: The diagram shows a red blood cell inside a capillary.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge-IGCSE-Biology-MARRY-JONES-4th-Ed
figures.shows: A line graph of measles cases in thousands (y-axis, 0 to 80 in steps of 10) against year (x-axis, 1944 to 2004, labelled every 10 years). From 1944 to about 1958 the line fluctuates widely between about 15 and 76 thousand, with a peak of about 76 thousand near 1958. From about 1959 to 1963 it stays between about 38 and 48 thousand. An arrow labelled 'vaccine introduced' points at the line at about 1963, after which it falls steeply to under 5 thousand by about 1967. It then stays low with small bumps near 1970, 1976 and 1988, and is close to zero from about 1990 to 2004.
figures.original: The graph shows the number of cases of measles in the USA between 1944 and 2004. Measles is caused by a virus. Vaccination for measles was introduced in the USA in 1963.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge-IGCSE-Biology-MARRY-JONES-4th-Ed

figures.original: The electron micrograph shows a group of influenza viruses.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge-IGCSE-Biology-MARRY-JONES-4th-Ed

An arrow shows the direction of the electrical impulse, pointing right into the axon ending.
figures.original: We can say that information travels along a neurone in an electrical form but travels between neurones in a chemical form. Explain this statement.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge-IGCSE-Biology-MARRY-JONES-4th-Ed
figures.shows: Three drawings of a method for investigating how light affects shoot growth. figures.original: Describe your results. You could include labelled diagrams if you like.

figures.original: The diagram shows the eye of a person who is relaxed.

figures.original: The photograph shows a tarsier.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge-IGCSE-Biology-MARRY-JONES-4th-Ed
figures.shows: Two side-by-side longitudinal section diagrams of primrose flowers, labelled 'pin-eyed' (left) and 'thrum-eyed' (right). figures.original: In a desert, kangaroo rats eat seeds of creosote bushes. Some of the kangaroo rats are eaten by kit foxes (Figure 18.6). Coyotes eat kit foxes.

figures.original: Carnivorous plants, such as sundews, often live in these places. These are plants that capture and digest insects, by producing proteases that they secrete onto the insect’s body (Figure 18.16). Suggest why carnivorous plants are usually found growing in waterlogged soils.

A red curve starts at the origin and rises steeply, then levels off at about 52-53 m/s by around 13 s and stays nearly constant to 20 s. A straight blue line starts at 20 m/s at 0 s and touches the red curve at about 5.5 s at roughly 42 m/s, reaching 70 m/s at 13 s. Black dashed lines mark 20 m/s horizontally from 0 to 13 s and 13 s vertically from 20 to 70 m/s.
figures.original: Look at Figure 2.20. What is the skydiver's acceleration at: a 0 s b 5.5 s?

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A table titled Table 2.8 with three columns: Station, Distance travelled/km, and Time taken/minutes. It lists five stations with their distances and times: Hornby 0 km, 0 min; Kirby Lonsdale 10 km, 30 min; Ingleton 20 km, 45 min; Dolphinholme 46 km, 60 min; Galgate 56 km, 80 min.
figures.original: Use the data in Table 2.8 to plot a distance–time graph for the train. Find the train's average speed between Kirby Lonsdale and Dolphinholme. Give your answer in km/h.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A ticker tape is drawn as two strips, one above the other, with a row of dots along each. Some dots are labelled with numbers: 0, 5, 10, 15 and 20 on the upper strip, and 25 and 30 on the lower strip. The dots are very close together near 0 and get steadily further apart along the tape. After about 10 the spacing looks roughly even, and it stays even to the end at 30.
figures.original: Copy and complete Table 2.10, using the ticker tape to help you.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A speed–time graph with time in s on the horizontal axis (0 to 120, labelled every 20) and speed in m/s on the vertical axis (0 to 40, labelled every 10). The line rises in a straight line from 0 at time 0 to about 43 m/s at about 15 s, stays flat at that speed until about 95 s, then falls in a straight line to 0 at 120 s.
figures.original: How is a constant velocity shown on the graph?

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A velocity–time graph with time in seconds on the horizontal axis (marked 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10) and velocity on the vertical axis (no numbers given). A straight line rises from the origin to a peak at about 7.2 s, and a dashed vertical line drops from the peak to the time axis. A steeper straight line then falls from the peak to zero velocity at 10 s.
figures.original: The velocity–time graph shows the performance of a Formula 1® racing car as it accelerates from rest for 7.33 seconds and then brakes, coming to a stop in 2.69 seconds. It covers a distance of 520 metres. What is the approximate maximum velocity of the car?

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: Three separate objects, each with a thick green arrow showing the direction of a force. (a) A golf ball on a red tee with a green arrow pointing to the right. (b) A car drawn with speed lines behind it, with a green arrow at its front pointing to the left. (c) An aeroplane seen from above, with a green arrow pointing up and to the left, across the fuselage.
figures.original: Figure 3.7 shows three objects that are moving. A force acts on each object. For each, say how its movement will change.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A photograph of a hammer thrower in a red outfit and blue shoes, spinning inside a throwing circle. She holds the handle of the hammer, and the wire stretches out to the left. The circle is surrounded by a tall red-posted protective cage with netting, with a stadium and spectators behind it. A bib on her front reads 'WANG'.
figures.original: Throwing the hammer is an Olympic sport (Figure 3.15), where the thrower spins around inside a circle while swinging a 'hammer'. Throwers spin as fast as they can before releasing the hammer. Looking down from above, sketch the path of the hammer moving in a circle followed by its path after it is released.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A table with three columns headed Force, Mass and Acceleration / m/s², and four rows. Row 1: Force a, mass 50 kg, acceleration 10. Row 2: force 112 N, mass 70 kg, acceleration b. Row 3: force 110 kN, mass c, acceleration 5. Row 4: force d, mass 15 g, acceleration 10. The letters a, b, c and d mark the missing values. The caption reads Table 3.3.
figures.original: Look at Table 3.3. Calculate the missing values a–d. Show your working.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A drawing of a tan wooden block, a long rectangular box, shown in perspective with its open end facing the lower left. A small green tennis ball sits at the lower left, and a black arrow runs from the ball to the block's end face, showing the ball travelling toward the block. There are no labels or values.
figures.original: Explain how the speed of the ball can be calculated using the principle of conservation of momentum. (Hint: this is a collision between the ball and the box.)

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: Four circles represent raindrops, labelled a, b, c and d, each with a vertical arrow pointing up from the top and a vertical arrow pointing down from the bottom. Drop a has 2.6 N up and 2.6 N down. Drop b has 1.4 N up and 1.8 N down. Drop c has 3.1 N up and 1.8 N down. Drop d has 0.8 N up and 2.6 N down.
figures.original: Which raindrop is slowing down?

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A drawing of a spanner on a bolt head at its upper left end. A dashed line along the spanner from the bolt to the handle end is labelled 50 cm. A horizontal dashed line at the top is labelled 30 cm, and a vertical dashed line on the right is labelled 40 cm. A green arrow at the handle end points down and to the left and is labelled "force provided by man = 30 N".
figures.original: A bolt is tightened by applying a turning force of 30 N to the end of the spanner (Figure 4.8). a Which of the three distance measurements should you use? b Use this distance to calculate the moment.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A horizontal brown ruler rests on a red triangular pivot located at its midpoint. A downward green arrow labelled 90 N acts on the left part of the ruler, 0.18 m to the left of the pivot. A downward green arrow labelled F acts near the right end, 0.07 m to the right of the pivot. Dashed vertical lines mark the positions of the two forces and the pivot.
figures.original: A uniform metre ruler is balanced at its midpoint (Figure 4.9). Calculate the unknown force F.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A side view of a horizontal trapdoor set in a floor, with a hinge at its left end. Three upward forces act on it: F1 = 300 N is a vertical arrow near the hinge, F2 = 200 N is a long arrow at the far right end that slants up and to the left, and F3 = 200 N is a vertical arrow at the far right end. The hinge and the trapdoor are labelled below the figure.
figures.original: Three different forces are pulling on a heavy trapdoor (Figure 4.6). Which force will have the biggest turning effect? Explain your answer.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A red double-decker bus labelled 'bus A' is tilted on a sloping platform, leaning over at a steep angle. A star marks the centre of gravity on the bus, and a label points to it reading 'centre of gravity'. A long vertical line with small marks runs beside the bus down to a red dot at the base, where the platform meets the flat ground.
figures.original: Buses and other vehicles have to be tilt-tested to an angle of at least 28 degrees from the vertical before they can carry passengers.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A photograph of a man in a light blue robe and white head covering pulling down on a long pole attached to a wooden lever (a shaduf) beside a river. The long wooden beam rests on a wooden frame pivot, with a woven basket or bucket hanging from a rope at one end and a counterweight of clay or mud at the other. Trees and plants are in the background.
figures.original: What is the advantage of making it take as much effort to push the bucket down as it does to pull it up?

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A horizontal brown ruler rests on a red triangular pivot. A 76 N downward force acts on the left side, 0.44 m to the left of the pivot. Two downward forces act on the right side: 125 N, drawn just to the right of the pivot, and 56 N, which is 0.34 m to the right of the pivot. The 0.44 m and 0.34 m distances are marked with dimension arrows between dashed vertical lines.
figures.original: Calculate the distance to the right of the pivot that the 125 N load needs to be placed for the ruler to be balanced.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A horizontal brown beam rests on a red triangular pivot located to the right of the beam's centre. A green block labelled 0.47 N hangs by a string from a point on the left part of the beam. The distance from the left end of the beam to the string is marked 0.13 m, and the distance from the left end to the pivot is marked 0.33 m, as shown by double-headed arrows.
figures.original: Calculate the anticlockwise moment of the 0.47 N force.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: Three drawings, labelled A, B and C, show a person standing on a sailboard floating on water. In A the sail lies flat on the water and the person leans back, pulling a rope attached to it. In B the sail is partly raised and the person still leans back and pulls the rope. In C the sail is upright and the person stands almost upright holding the mast. A point P is marked on the board at the base of the sail in each drawing.
figures.original: a As the sail is pulled up from A to C, how does the force needed vary? Explain your answer.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A windsurfer stands on a board floating on wavy water, holding a sail. A horizontal arrow labelled 'wind force' points left from the sail, and a vertical double-headed arrow labelled '1.5 m' marks the height of that arrow above the pivot. The point P is marked on the board at the base of the mast, and a downward arrow labelled 'weight' acts from the board.
figures.original: c Calculate how far to the right of the pivot the windsurfer has to move his centre of gravity.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: Two drawings of an angle-poise lamp on a base. Each has a vertical stem with a pivot at the top, a lamp arm, and a cord running vertically down from the pivot to a spring near the base. In the left drawing the arm is horizontal, the lamp hangs at its left end, a 25 cm distance is marked from the line of the 3.75 N downward weight to the pivot, and in the right drawing the arm is tilted upward to the left with the lamp raised and a 3.75 N downward weight arrow. The vertical cord is labelled 'pivot' in both drawings.
figures.original: The diagram shows an angle-poise lamp. The light is at the end of an arm. The arm can be moved about the pivot. The cord passes vertically down to a stretched spring.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: Four panels (a, b, c, d) each show a bicycle chainring with a crank arm and pedal in a different position, with a downward force of 500 N on the pedal. In a, the pedal is up and to the left, with a 5 cm horizontal distance marked at the pedal and a 14 cm vertical distance marked near the crank. In b, the crank points straight up and is labelled 15 cm. In c, the crank points horizontally left and is labelled 15 cm. In d, the crank points left and slightly up, with 5 cm marked vertically at the pedal and 14 cm marked horizontally.
figures.original: The pictures show different positions of a bicycle pedal. Which position would result in the biggest turning force?

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A plan view of a gate drawn as a long horizontal bar with a pivot at its left end, labelled 'pivot', and a block under each end. Four force arrows are labelled A, B, C and D. A is a short upward arrow close to the pivot. B is a medium-length upward arrow about halfway along the gate. C is a long arrow at the far right end, pointing up and to the left at an angle. D is the longest arrow, pointing straight up at the far right end.
figures.original: This is a plan view of a gate that will swing open about the pivot shown. Also shown are the positions for a motor and the direction they will move the gate. The length of the arrows indicates the size of the force. Choose the arrow that will swing the gate open the quickest.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A horizontal beam bridge rests on two pairs of sloping legs, one at the left end and one at the right end. A toy steam train sits on the bridge roughly midway between the supports. An upward arrow at the left support is labelled 'force X', and an upward arrow at the right support is labelled 'force Y'. A downward arrow from the train is labelled 'weight of train 8 N'.
figures.original: A toy train is crossing a bridge. The centre of gravity of the train is mid-way between the supports. Which row of the table shows the correct values of the contact forces at X and Y?

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A horizontal bar (a ruler) is marked with a scale from 0 cm at the left end to 100 cm at the right end. A triangular pivot sits under the bar at the 55 cm mark. A 50 g mass hangs from a string looped around the bar at the 85 cm mark.
figures.original: A 1.0 metre wooden ruler is damaged and no longer uniform. The mass of the ruler is 11.5 g. The ruler is balanced on a pivot with a 50 g mass as shown. Where is the centre of gravity of the ruler?

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: Two parts, a and b, show a cyclist seen from behind. In a, the cyclist is upright, with a green arrow labelled 'weight' pointing down and a green arrow labelled 'contact force' pointing up at the ground. In b, the cyclist leans to one side while turning, shown by a red dashed curved arrow. The arrows are 'weight' pointing down, 'contact force' pointing up and 'friction' pointing sideways along the ground.
figures.original: Figure 4.24 shows the forces acting on a cyclist.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A table titled Table 5.2 with three columns: Load/N, Length/cm and Extension/cm. Load and length values are printed for nine rows, and the Extension column has 0 in the first row and is blank for all the other rows.
figures.original: Table 5.2 shows the results of an experiment to stretch an elastic cord. Copy and complete the table, and draw a graph to represent this data (with load on the vertical axis).

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: Two photographs labelled a and b show the same multicoloured bowl made of swirled orange, red, blue, yellow, green and white material, resting on a grey speckled surface. In a, the bowl is a regular, round, upright bowl. In b, the bowl has sagged and deformed into a flattened, saddle-like shape with a raised, wavy middle.
figures.original: Using your knowledge of physics, explain how this can happen.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A table with two columns headed 'Load/N' and 'Length/m'. It has six rows of values: 0.0 N with 1.396 m, 2.6 N with 1.422 m, 5.3 N with 1.448 m, 7.9 N with 1.475 m, 10.6 N with 1.501 m, and 13.2 N with 1.536 m.
figures.original: The results of an experiment to stretch a spring are shown in Table 5.3. Use the results to plot a load–extension graph. On your graph, mark the limit of proportionality and state the value of the load at that point.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A book held in two hands and bent into an arch, with the spine on the left and the page edges fanning out at the right end. The front cover is the outer, upper curved surface and the back cover is the inner, lower curved surface. A short red dashed line at the right end marks the difference in length between the front and back covers if the book were a solid block of paper.
labels: This would be the difference in length between the front and back covers if the book was a solid block of paper.
figures.original: Now bend it into the shape of an arch with the spine on the left-hand side as shown in Figure 5.11.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A car hydraulic braking system. A foot pushes a pedal connected to an effort piston in a cylinder, with an arrow showing the direction of push. Brake fluid in a pipe runs to a caliper with two load pistons on either side of a brake disc, with arrows pointing inwards. The brake disc is attached to an axle and the wheel with its tyre. A second pipe branches off labelled 'to other brakes'.
figures.original: Car braking systems multiply forces. In the diagram below, there are three pistons: one effort piston and two load pistons.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: Two drawings of a coil spring hung from a fixed support. On the left the spring hangs with nothing attached, and its length from the support is marked as 8 cm. On the right the spring hangs from the support with a cylindrical mass attached at the bottom, and its length is marked as 18 cm.
figures.original: This spring obeys Hooke's law and stretches from 8 cm to 18 cm when a force of 20 N is applied.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: Four table legs, labelled A, B, C and D, each drawn standing on a flat floor line. Leg A is a vertical leg that widens into a flared, bulging foot with a flat base. Leg B is a vertical leg that narrows and then spreads out into a wide, rounded flared base. Leg C is a leg that tapers to a narrow point at the floor. Leg D is a leg fitted with a small round castor wheel at the bottom.
figures.original: Heavy furniture sometimes marks the floor on which it stands. Four tables of the same weight each have four legs. The figure shows part of a leg from each table. Which table is least likely to mark the floor?

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: Four circles labelled A, B, C and D, each representing a submarine, with small arrows drawn around the outside. In A, the arrows all point inward toward the circle and are about the same length all the way round. In B, the arrows point inward, and those at the top and bottom are drawn slightly longer than the others. In C, the arrows point inward and are longer at the top and shorter at the bottom. In D, the arrows point inward and are longer at the bottom and shorter at the top.
figures.original: Which diagram shows the pressure acting on the submarine that is not moving?

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A graph with Load / N on the vertical axis and Extension / cm on the horizontal axis. Four straight lines labelled A, B, C and D all start at the origin. A is the steepest, then B, then C, and D is the shallowest. No numerical values are printed on either axis.
figures.original: Look at the graph. Which material is the stiffest?

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: Two tall open-topped containers labelled A and B stand side by side. Each has a tap at the bottom, and a pipe joins the two taps. A vertical double-headed arrow at the left of container A is labelled 80 cm and spans from the base up the side of the container. Container A appears empty. Container B has a faint line partway up, which may mark a water level.
figures.original: The diagram shows two containers that store rainwater. The containers have taps. A pipe joins the taps. The taps are closed. Both containers have a base of area 0.07 m².

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A table titled 'ACTIVITY 6.3 Moon flight high jump' with columns: High jump record / m, Athlete, Height of athlete / m, Year. Men: 2.45, Javier Sotomayor (Cuba), 1.95, 1993. Women: 2.09, Stefka Kostadinova (Bulgaria), 1.80, 1987.
figures.topic: Chapter 6: Energy transformations and energy transfers
figures.original: Table 6.4 lists the current world records for the high jump. Predict what the high jump record would be on the lunar surface.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A side-on drawing of a roller coaster track supported by a criss-cross lattice, with a small car at the bottom left on the upward slope. The track rises to a high peak P, falls to a low dip Q, rises to a smaller peak R, then falls to ground level at S. A double-headed arrow at P is labelled 50 m and shows the height of P above the ground. Another arrow at R shows the height of R above the ground and is labelled with a question mark.
figures.topic: Chapter 6: Energy transformations and energy transfers
figures.original: This diagram shows an amusement park roller coaster ride (not drawn to scale).

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: Five numbered panels (1 to 5) show an athlete at successive stages of a pole vault. Each panel has a vertical bar (the crossbar upright) and a light blue landing mat on the right. In 1 the athlete runs carrying a horizontal pole, in 2 the pole tip is planted at the base of the upright, in 3 the pole is bent with the athlete swinging upward, in 4 the pole is straight and upright as the athlete passes over the bar, and in 5 the athlete lies on the mat with the pole fallen on the ground.
figures.topic: Chapter 6: Energy transformations and energy transfers
figures.original: Snapshots (labelled 1–5) of an athlete at different stages of the pole vault are as shown in Figure 6.17. Between each snapshot, the energy is transferred between stores.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: Two side-by-side drawings of a ballistic pendulum, labelled 'before' and 'after'. Before: a block hangs from a pivot on a vertical rod, and a small dot (the projectile) to its left moves right with speed labelled V_P. After: the projectile is embedded in the block, which swings up along a dashed outline to the right with speed labelled V_B, and the vertical rise of the block is marked as height h.
figures.original: Scientists use a ballistic pendulum to work out the speed of a projectile that hits it. The block has a mass of 4.7 kg and moves with an initial speed of 1.24 m/s when it is hit.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A table with three column headings: 'Description', 'Name of energy' and 'Store or transfer'. The Description column has eight filled-in rows, and the other two columns are empty for the learner to complete.
labels: energy carried by an electric current
energy in the nucleus of an atom
energy escaping from a hot object
figures.topic: Chapter 6: Energy transformations and energy transfers
figures.original: Copy and complete the table. For each description, write down the name of the associated energy and state whether it is a store or transfer.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A Sankey-style energy transfer diagram. A wide grey arrow labelled 'energy input' on the left splits into two arrows: a wide arrow pointing right to 'useful energy output', and a thinner arrow curving downward to 'waste energy'.
figures.original: This diagram represents an energy transfer. Copy and complete the following two word equations for this energy change:

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A map of Sanghera Island with north arrow at top, showing contour-shaded hills with spot heights, streams, forest patches in the north, two hot springs, and dotted tracks. A scale bar shows 1 km. Spot heights are 278, 338, 571, 778 and 812.
figures.original: Sanghera Island (Figure 7.10) is a remote fictitious island.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A table with three columns headed 'Energy resource', 'Non-renewable' and 'Renewable'. The first column lists ten energy resources: wave power, hydroelectricity, geothermal, coal, nuclear energy, oil, solar energy, natural gas, tidal energy and wind energy. The Non-renewable and Renewable columns are empty.
figures.original: Copy the table. In the first blank column, put a tick by any three resources that are non-renewable. In the second blank column, put a tick by any three resources that are renewable.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A table with columns 'Type of power station', 'For', 'Against' and 'Overall score'. The wind farm row has For 2, Against 4 and Overall score −2. The nuclear row has For 7, Against 3 and Overall score 4.
figures.original: Subtract your vote for the opposition from your vote for the advocates to get an overall score. Two examples are given in Table 7.1.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A girl pushes a wooden box up a sloping ramp. A green arrow pointing right from the box is labelled 200 N, and a green arrow pointing straight down from the box is labelled 400 N. The ramp's sloping length is marked 2.5 m, and its vertical height is marked 0.75 m.
figures.original: a How much work does she do in raising the box? b How much g.p.e. does the box gain?

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A washing machine sits on a straight wooden ramp that slopes upward to the right, from the ground to the floor of a trailer (removal van). A double-headed arrow along the ramp is labelled 1.6 m, and an arrow pointing up the slope is labelled 440 N. A vertical double-headed arrow on the trailer shows its floor height above the ground as 0.80 m.
figures.original: A man is trying to move his washing machine into the back of a removal van. The washing machine has a weight of 650 N and the floor of the removal van is 0.80 metres above the ground (Figure 8.9).

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A gymnast in a white sleeveless top and long white trousers holds himself motionless on two gymnastic rings, with his arms stretched out horizontally to each side and his body hanging straight down. Spectators sit in stands behind him. No labels or values are printed.
figures.original: But is he doing any work from a physics point of view?

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A table with four columns: Speed / m/s, Thinking distance / m, Braking distance / m, Stopping distance / m. It has six rows: 8.9, 6, 6, 12; 13.4, 9, 14, 23; 17.9, 12, 24, 36; 22.3, 15, 38, 53; 26.8, 18, 55, 73; 31.3, 21, 75, 96.
figures.original: Assume that the mass of the car is 1500 kg and the braking force is 10 000 N. Show that you get nearly the same braking distance as in Table 8.1.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A brown horse on the left pulls a rope that runs up and over a spoked pulley wheel at the upper right. The rope's other end holds an orange block on the right. The block is drawn at two heights: a lower one labelled 33 000 lb and a higher one raised by Δh = 1 foot, with an upward arrow and a brace between them. A stopwatch symbol is labelled Δt = 1 min.
figures.original: 7 One horsepower is the power output of one horse when it lifts a mass of 33 000 lb of water through a height of one foot in one minute as shown in Figure 8.12.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A right-angled slope (incline) rising to the right, with a man pushing a pram up it. A 150 N arrow points up along the slope. The slope length is labelled 20 m with a double-headed arrow along the underside of the slope. The vertical height at the right-hand end is labelled 10 m with a double-headed arrow.
figures.original: A man pushes a 25 kg pram up a slope as shown in the diagram. He pushes with a force of 150 N along the 20 m slope. How much energy is dissipated as thermal energy?

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A cross-section of a subway station. A row of terraced houses stands at street level, and a vertical shaft with a people symbol runs from the street down to a train at the platform. The platform and train sit at a higher level than the tunnel on each side. The tunnel slopes down on both sides of the station to a lower level.
figures.original: The diagram shows a section through a subway station. The track at the station platform is designed to be higher up than the track in the tunnels. The driver uses brakes to stop the train at the platform and a motor to make the train set off. What is the advantage of having the platform higher up than the track in the tunnels? Explain your answer in terms of the work done by the brakes and the motor.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A drawing of a syringe tilted diagonally, with the needle tip at the upper right and the plunger with its flange at the lower left. labels: An extensive area of flat land which is higher than the land around it. Close contours surround a wide area that has no or few contours.
Low land between hills or mountains. It usually has a river flowing through it. Contours form a U- or V-shape that points towards high land.
A high round piece of land, not as large as a mountain. Contours form a circle or oval shape.
An area of land that sticks out like a finger from the side of a mountain or hill. Contours form a U- or V-shape that points away from high land.
A high, steep, rocky slope formed by erosion or earth movements. Contours are on top of or nearly on top of each other.
Long narrow hilltop. Closely spaced contours form a long sausage shape.
Two areas of high land with a dip between them. It is shown by two circular or sausage-shaped contours with a gap between them.

A high round piece of land, not as large as a mountain. Contours form a circle or oval shape.
An area of land that sticks out like a finger from the side of a mountain or hill. Contours form a U- or V-shape that points away from high land.
A high, steep, rocky slope formed by erosion or earth movements. Contours are on top of or nearly on top of each other.
Long narrow hilltop. Closely spaced contours form a long sausage shape.
Two areas of high land with a dip between them. It is shown by two circular or sausage-shaped contours with a gap between them.

HIV destroys CD4 cells which is a specific type of white blood cell that plays a large role in helping the body fight disease. The body’s immune system weakens as more CD4 cells are killed. It is possible to have an HIV infection for years before it progresses to AIDS.
People infected with HIV progress to AIDS when their CD4 count falls below 200 or they experience an AIDS-defining complication.

Parts of the text are shaded grey and enclosed in square brackets, marking the regions where editing is allowed.
labels: There are many reasons for singling out children's rights in a separate human rights Convention:
Children are neither the possessions of parents nor of the state, nor are they mere people-in-the-making; they have equal status as members of the human family.
Children start life as totally dependent beings

Children must rely on adults for the nurture and guidance they need to grow towards independence. Such nurture is ideally found from adults in children's families, but when primary adult caregivers cannot meet children's needs, it is up to the State as the primary duty bearer to find an alternative in the best interests of the child.

figures.shows: A typographic poster on a dark blue background that shows visual hierarchy in text. The word "YOU" is in very large cyan letters, and "WILL READ THIS FIRST." is in very large white bold capitals. A small line beside "YOU" reads "At some point you may come back to read this line or maybe not." Below is a medium cyan line, "And then you will read this line next." At the bottom is a small white paragraph of body text, with a cyan side note separated by a vertical line.
labels: At some point you may come back to read this line or maybe not.
And then you will read this line next.

You will go back to read this body copy if you want to know more. It takes the most effort to read because it has a lot of text in a small font in a light weight with tight line spacing. Many people will skip paragraphs like this unless if they aren't engaged right away. This is why it's important to draw attention to your message using visual hierarchy.
You'll probably read this before the paragraph.

Pressure in kilograms per square centimeter

figures.shows: Two panels with graphs and cylinders. Top, Boyle's Law: volume in liters against pressure in kilograms per square centimeter (axis 0 to 40), with a blue decreasing curve and four cylinders filled with gas at pressures 10, 20, 30 and 40, marked at volume levels 1, 1/2, 1/3 and 1/4. A blue arrow points down, labelled 'Compressing the gas'. Bottom, Charles' Law: volume in liters against temperature in kelvins (0 to 400), with a red straight line rising from the origin and four cylinders filled to increasing levels at 100, 200, 300 and 400 K, marked at 1/4, 1/2, 3/4 and 1 liters. A red arrow points up, labelled 'Increasing the temperature'. Each panel has a text description of its law.
labels: If a gas is held at a constant temperature, the volume is inversely proportional to the pressure. Compressing a gas to half of its initial volume doubles its pressure.
Pressure in kilograms per square centimeter
If a gas is held at a constant pressure, the volume is directly proportional to the absolute temperature. Heating a gas to double its original temperature doubles its volume.

labels: What is the purpose of the market research?
What does it want to find out? What information will be needed? What action will be taken as a result of the research? This will affect the type of market research undertaken.
Decide on the most suitable method of research

Will more than one method be necessary? Will just secondary research be sufficient or will primary research be needed as well? The cost of the research and the time required will need to be taken into account.
Decide on the size of sample needed and who is going to be asked

How big will the sample size need to be to keep costs down but get a sufficiently accurate result? Which different groups of people will need to be included in the survey? Different age groups? Different income groups?
Collate the data and analyse the results
The information will need to be put together and the data analysed. What does it seem to show?
Produce a report of the findings

A report will need to be produced showing the findings. Included in the report will be a summary of the research findings and conclusions drawn based on these results. Recommendations should be made as to what actions are necessary as a result of the research; these should be based on the conclusions.

3 Decide if the company will be able to sell enough for the product to be a success

The Marketing department now looks in detail at the remaining ideas. It assesses how large it thinks the sales would be and the likely size of the market share. A break-even analysis (see Chapter 19) is carried out to see how many sales would be needed to cover costs. Development costs should also be included.

A prototype allows the Operations department to see how a product could be manufactured. It also allows them to foresee any problems with the manufacturing process. Many large companies use computer simulations for part of this process.
5 Launch the product in one area to test the market

The product is launched on to one small part of the market. This allows the company to see how well the product sells without committing large amounts of money for a national launch. If the product does not sell well, it can be altered or scrapped without too much harm to the company.
6 Go to a full launch of the product to the whole market
The product is launched on to the main market. This will probably be the national market to begin with. Later it could be exported.

figures.shows: A tree diagram with a teal box labelled 'Economics' at the top, branching into two boxes below. The left box defines Microeconomics as the study of individual markets, and the right box defines Macroeconomics as the study of the whole economy or group of economies. Each box also gives an example topic.
labels: Microeconomics is the study of individual markets. It looks at the behaviour and decisions of households (consumers) and firms (businesses), and how they interact. An example of a microeconomics topic is the factors that explain why consumers buy some goods and not others.

Macroeconomics is the study of the whole economy or group of economies. Macroeconomics also looks at how consumers and firms interact but on a broader level. Macroeconomics is likely to include some form of government involvement. For example, macroeconomics covers the reasons why one economy grows at a faster rate than another economy.

figures.shows: A cross-section diagram of the rock cycle. A mountain of surface rock sits above igneous and metamorphic rock, with sedimentary rock by the sea and magma deep below. Red arrows show the numbered processes: 1 weathering and erosion, 2 transportation, 3 sedimentation, 4 heat and pressure, 5 melting, 6 cooling, 7 uplift. A numbered key of seven steps is printed at the top right.
labels: 1. Weathering and erosion break off fragments of surface rock.
2. The eroded rock is transported to another location.
3. The fragments of rock are deposited and build up in layers. As the layers build up, the lower layers are compacted into sedimentary rock.
4. Sedimentary and igneous rocks subjected to heat and pressure underground form metamorphic rocks.
5. At higher temperatures rocks melt to form magma.
6. Magma cools to form igneous rock.
7. Movements in the Earth raise rocks to the surface via a process called uplift.

figures.shows: A screenshot of a Microsoft Word window (Home tab, Courier New 10.5) showing a document headed 'Winter weather forces schools to close' with paragraphs about snow on Monday February 2nd 2009 and a 'School closures' heading. A two-column table headed County and Closed lists the number of schools closed in each county, with a blank extra column cell mark to the right of the table. Below it are paragraphs about the table and children playing in the snow.
labels: Winter weather forces schools to close

On Monday February 2nd 2009 the South East of England was hit by snow. I know this is not unusual in many parts of the world, but it was interesting to watch the whole region grind to a virtual standstill. At the time of writing this article the major London airports of Heathrow, Gatwick and London City were all closed. Stansted airport had been closed but has just had one runway reopened. Travel chaos has ensued, the M25 is closed in many places and many schools throughout the country have been closed.
The dramatic change in the weather has meant that a number of areas are experiencing transport problems. This means that many schools across the country have been closed.

figures.shows: A word-processing document with five paragraphs, shown with formatting marks (dots for spaces, pilcrow marks at paragraph ends), demonstrating different paragraph indents. The first paragraph has its first line indented; the second is indented as a whole (an indented paragraph); the third is a normal paragraph with no indents; the fourth is a hanging paragraph with the first line at the margin and later lines indented; the fifth begins with 'Good use', then a tab arrow, then hanging-indented text.
labels: This paragraph contains indented text. This means that the left margin on the first line is indented from the rest of the paragraph. The top margin setting on the ruler is indented to the right of the lower margin setting.

The whole of this paragraph has been indented from the left margin and is called an indented paragraph. This is sometimes used to show sub-text within a document, or for showing a quotation from another author.
This paragraph is a normal paragraph with no indents and no hanging first line. The margin settings on the ruler are directly above each other.

This paragraph is called a hanging paragraph. This means that the first line of the paragraph is aligned to the margin and all other lines are left hanging. The bottom margin setting on the ruler is indented to the right of the top margin setting.

One really good use of a hanging paragraph is for short titles like this one to be followed by the relevant text. By setting a tab stop on the first line, the short title can be used as a heading. This layout can give each heading a powerful effect on the page, without any other text enhancement like enlarging or emboldening the text.

labels: Select the source and destination of the data
Specify the source of the definition of the objects.
Specify how and where you want to store the data in the current database.
We will not import table relationships, calculated columns, validation rules, default values, and columns of certain legacy data types such as OLE Object.
Search for 'Import' in Microsoft Access Help for more information.
Import the source data into a new table in the current database.

If the specified table does not exist, Access will create it. If the specified table already exists, Access might overwrite its contents with the imported data. Changes made to the source data will not be reflected in the database.
Append a copy of the records to the table:

If the specified table does not exist, Access will add the records to the table. If the specified table does not exist, Access will create it. Changes made to the source data will not be reflected in the database.
Link to the data source by creating a linked table.
Access will create a table that will maintain a link to the source data. You cannot change or delete data that is linked to a text file. However, you can add new records.
