figures.shows: A text box headed 'D Diversification' contains a farmer's quoted account of how EU policy shaped his farm. He set aside 15% of his wheat area and claimed EU Area Payments and payments for crops such as oil-seed rape and linseed. He also grows strawberries and raspberries as pick-your-own near the main road, runs a Caravan Club site for five caravans, and claims grants for hedges, trees, ponds and a 10-metre uncultivated strip around field edges.
labels: Since I bought the farm much of what I do has been influenced by the EU. I used to grow a lot more wheat but, because of overproduction in the EU, we were asked to set aside 15% of our usual wheat area. For this we could claim an EU Area Payment and then another payment for growing a crop the EU did want on the same land such as oil-seed rape and linseed. I have also diversified into growing fruit – mainly strawberries and raspberries – close to the main road as a pick-your-own (PYO) enterprise. I now use land for a Caravan Club site for five caravans. Without the EU grants, subsidies and payments for these activities, farmers would be bankrupt; people just wouldn't pay the full price to cover costs. I still claim grants for planting hedges and trees, creating ponds and for not farming a 10-metre strip around the edge of many fields which encourages wildlife. After all it's in the farmers' interests to look after the environment.

labels: Darfur – a difficult area to live and work in

In western and central Darfur there is a short wet season where, for a few months of the year, the dusty brown environment changes to a lush green. In normal years pearl millet can be harvested by November and the dry stalks fed to livestock during the long dry season.
Nyala is the capital of southern Darfur. It is a town full of government officials, with food in the market and cafés. Yet, close by, the needs of 40 000 refugees in tented camps are ignored.
The northern Libyan desert is hot with almost constant dry winds. Rain may not fall for years. 1.5 million people live here in drought conditions. Locusts are a threat, too.
The river Nile only flows through east Sudan so agriculture can be developed there using irrigation even with low amounts of rainfall.
In a small area in the south, average annual rainfall can total 700 mm, so vegetation can grow here all the year round.

figures.shows: A page titled 'Food shortages – different causes' with a world map. Countries shaded red are the Philippines, Venezuela, Yemen, Afghanistan, Zimbabwe and Syria. Around the map are seven short news-style panels, each with a flag and text giving the cause of food shortage in that country: Philippines (typhoon), El Salvador (floods), Yemen (locust plague), Venezuela (protests and violence), Zimbabwe (land taken over, drought), Afghanistan (drought, mountain access), Syria (civil war).
labels: Over 1.6 million need food aid in Zimbabwe

It was once the 'bread basket' of Africa, people in Zimbabwe need food aid. Many farmers have had their land taken over by the government and many fields are going to waste. Drought, rising prices and a lack of investment in fertilisers and machinery are also being blamed.
Access for food and water a problem in Afghanistan

Ongoing drought and the continuing problem of difficult access into the mountains means that almost 9 million people face food shortages. The wheat crop failed due to a lack of rain. Transporting food and water for irrigation into the mountains is an almost impossible task.
Civil war puts Syria children at risk

Lack of access to food, rising food prices and a collapse in food production have put children in Syria at risk of malnutrition. More than 4 million people – half of whom are children – are unable to produce or buy enough food as the war continues. Many have fled to neighbouring countries such as Iran where food supply cannot provide for the extra refugees.
Food shortage major issue after typhoon hits Philippines

Food shortages are the greatest threat that survivors of typhoon Haiyan face. All the coconut plantations have been destroyed. Food aid will run out in three months but the next coconut harvest cannot be for another year.
Floods in El Salvador have left over 50 000 people homeless and without food. About 10 000 people are in need of food aid after heavy rains washed away crops.
Locust plague aggravates food shortage in Yemen

A plague of locusts has devastated crops in Yemen. The country already faces a food shortage due to poor investment in farming and droughts. 75% of the people depend on farming for their food but it is either too dry or, when the rains come, the locusts can breed and eat any crops that are grown.
Food shortages trigger protests in Venezuela

Six weeks of violence against the government has plunged the country into crisis. Rationing and a fingerprinted ID card have been introduced to stop people stockpiling food. In state-run shops people queue for hours for basic food such as flour, cooking oil and chicken.

figures.shows: A box titled 'Why locate at Pipri?' has a table with columns 'Factors influencing location' and 'Reason' (blank). Rows are PHYSICAL (header), Site, Natural routes, Raw materials, HUMAN (header), Capital, Energy, Labour, Markets, Transport. Around it are eight rounded text boxes describing the harbour at Port Qasim, imported raw materials and water, electricity capacity, local labour, flat cheap land, USSR assistance, rail and road links, and steel-using industries in Karachi and Taxila.
labels: Port Qasim has a natural harbour that can deal with imports of materials and exports of steel to the countries neighbouring the Arabian Sea and east and west of the Indian Ocean. The 2.5 km long seawater channel is kept navigable for ships.

Iron ore, manganese and most of the coking coal can be imported through Port Qasim. Limestone, needed as a flux, can be brought by road from the nearby Makli Hills near Thatta. Large quantities of water required for making steel can be brought from Lake Haleji, 50 km to the east (saltwater is not suitable).

Port Qasim and Karachi had the highest electricity-generating capacity in the country. Pipri thermal power station produced 21% and Koranga thermal power station produced 15% of the total. Karachi also has a nuclear power station.
Plenty of skilled and unskilled cheap labour was available locally from Karachi.
Flat, cheap unused land was available at Pipri near Gharo Creek.
The former USSR (now Russia) provided economic assistance in the form of technical expertise, finance and capital.
Pipri was connected to the main Karachi–Kotri railway. Metalled roads also connected this area to the main road system

Many steel-using industries were located in Karachi such as tool-making. It supplies rolled sheets, galvanised sheets, pig iron and coal tar to the rest of the country. Over half the steel is used in the Punjab at Taxila where many factories were established with Chinese finance in 1979.

figures.shows: A text source titled 'Al Maha Desert Resort and Spa, Dubai, United Arab Emirates', labelled Source C. It has paragraphs describing the resort's location in a 225 km² conservation reserve, its 37 suites of 75 m², its facilities, and its water and recycling practices. A photograph of a desert at sunset with palm trees, animals and a pool of water sits beside the text.
labels: Al Maha Desert Resort and Spa
Al Maha Desert Resort and Spa, Dubai, United Arab Emirates

The Al Maha Desert Resort and Spa is at the centre of the 225 km² Dubai Desert Conservation Reserve in the Arabian Desert, built in old-style Arabian architecture. Conservation of the desert's ecosystem was a part of the development project. A wildlife reserve was developed which has 33 indigenous mammal and reptile species, 100 bird species, and nearly 300 Arabian oryx.

The 37 suites each measure 75 m² and contain a king-size bed, minibar, bathroom with a king-size bath, walk-in-shower and vanity areas. The main restaurant is cool and airy, and serves international cuisines. It has a shaded terrace with views of the reserve and mountains. The resort also offers a personal dining facility in a secluded spot in the sand dunes within the reserve.

The Al Maha's spa and fitness facility overlooks the mountains, and includes treatment rooms, a sauna, a steam room and a jacuzzi. There is a swimming pool and gymnasium and the services of a personal trainer. Al Maha has a library featuring original artworks and paintings, and is furnished with rustic furniture and woven traditional rugs.
Guests can rest in Majlis, a traditional Arabic seating area. There is a souvenir shop selling a range of antiques and artefacts.

The resort protects one of the largest underground water reservoirs of the United Arab Emirates. Before it was turned into a resort the land was used for farming and the water was used for irrigation. Since the opening of the hotel there has been no reduction in the quality and level of the water. All glass, plastic, cans and paper used in the hotel are recycled and all kitchen oils and organic wastes are carefully disposed of.

figures.shows: Two boxed letters to the editor under the title 'Letters to the Editor'. The left letter, headed 'Mayor's disgraceful behaviour' and signed Maria Alonso, strongly opposes a hotel and eco-theme park, using emotive words such as horrified, gigantic, choke, chaos, monstrosities and tragedy (shown in bold). The right letter, headed 'Getting the facts right' and signed José Moreno, supports the hotel, saying it will be built outside the town, cars will be banned from the centre, the park is educational, 120 jobs will be created, and a similar development raised local shop revenues five-fold.
labels: Our mayor's behaviour has horrified our desperate residents. We were only made aware of his underhand tactics at the beginning of Wednesday's disgraceful meeting.

The truth of the matter is that this gigantic hotel and the so-called eco-theme park will bring floods of visitors to our town. Their cars and buses will choke our narrow streets. The result will be chaos! I believe that one hotel will lead to other monstrosities springing up in every little corner of our beloved Bellavista. What a terrible tragedy!
Let us all campaign to defeat this dangerous and destructive proposal.
As a recent resident of Bellavista, I can naturally understand the controversy caused by the proposal to build a hotel. Those who oppose it should carefully consider the facts.

This hotel will definitely be built outside the town and cars will, as at present, be absolutely banned from the centre. The eco-theme park is educational and will be strictly targeted at hard-working, well-behaved children. Finally, this developer has promised to create 120 jobs for local people. A similar development in the town where I used to live has increased the revenues of local shops five-fold.
The peace and prosperity of our town seem safely protected.

labels: Trembling granddaughter sensed a strange pride pour through her body.

Personification is used to compare the feeling of pride to a liquid – 'pour' suggests a large, fast-moving quantity. The effect of this is to show the reader how much the granddaughter has developed from a hesitant girl to one whose positive emotions now move freely and quickly through her.
She stroked trust and courage, skill and dignity into trembling granddaughter.

figures.shows: A shaded box titled 'Forming plurals' that lists rules for making plural nouns. Each rule is followed by examples: add 's' (table/tables, tree/trees, cat/cats); add 'es' after s, sh, ch, x, z (Bus/buses, bush/bushes, branch/branches, box/boxes, buzz/buzzes); consonant + o (hero/heroes, zero/zeros); vowel + o (patio/patios); consonant + y (story/stories); vowel + y (journey/journeys, monkey/monkeys); f or fe (roof/roofs, wolf/wolves); exceptions that change vowels (man/men, mouse/mice); nouns that don't change (sheep/sheep, salmon/salmon).
labels: To form the plural of most nouns simply add 's'.
If the noun ends with 's', 'sh', 'ch', 'x' or 'z' add 'es'.
Examples: Bus/buses bush/bushes branch/branches box/boxes buzz/buzzes
If the noun ends with a consonant and 'o' add 's' or 'es' (there are no rules for which one, you have to learn them).
If the noun ends with a vowel and 'o' add 's'.
If the noun ends with a consonant and 'y' change the 'y' to an 'i' and add 'es'.
If the noun ends with a vowel and 'y' just add 's'.
If the noun ends with 'f' or 'fe' either remove f and add 'ves' or simply add 's' (there is no rule for which, you simply have to learn them).
There are exceptions to the rules. Some nouns change vowels or consonants.
Some nouns don't change at all!

The Unique Product Code (UPC) check digit is used with 13 digit barcodes. It is the last digit shown on a barcode. The algorithm for calculating the check digit is:
1 Add all the digits in even numbered positions together.
2 Multiply the result (1) above by 3.
3 Add all the digits in odd numbered positions together.
4 Add results (2) and (3)

figures.original: Drop-down boxes allow a user to select from a list that appears when the drop-down box appears on screen. Only one option can be chosen. It then goes through these steps in order: 'Light sensor takes reading' (input shape), 'Analogue data converted to digital value', 'Value sent to microprocessor', and 'Microprocessor compares value to a pre-set range'. A decision diamond 'Is value in range?' follows. The N branch loops back to the light sensor reading step. The Y branch leads to 'Signal sent to actuator to turn street light on/off' (output shape), which also loops back to the light sensor reading step.
labels: Analogue data converted to digital value
Microprocessor compares value to a pre-set range
Signal sent to actuator to turn street light on/off
figures.original:
A real-life example of a control technology in operation would be an automated street light. This may include the following stages:
• A light sensor will constantly monitor the level of light present in the surrounding environment.
• The analogue data from the reading will be converted to a digital value by an analogue to digital converter.
• The digital signal is sent to a microprocessor and the microprocessor will compare the value to a pre-set range.

figures.shows: A flowchart of the fetch–execute cycle with interrupt handling. It runs from 'start execution of the program' to 'fetch instruction', then 'execute instruction', then the decision 'is there an interrupt?'. If yes, it goes to 'service the interrupt'; if no, it skips that step. Both paths rejoin at a point marked by a callout 'return to the interrupted program', then reach the decision 'any more instructions?'. If yes, an arrow loops back to before 'fetch instruction'; if no, the flow ends at 'end program'.

figures.original: If the OS is to manage interrupts, the sequence in Figure 3.1.4 is modified as shown in Figure 3.1.5. After the execution of an instruction, the processor checks to see if an interrupt has occurred. If so, the OS services the interrupt if it is more important than the task already being carried out.

Scientists estimate that 1 out of 3 seabirds have plastic in their stomachs.
Around the world, 8 million tonnes of plastic enters the ocean every year. That's the same as a dumper truck of rubbish every minute of every day.
Scientists estimate it will take 400 years for a plastic ring holder to break up into tiny pieces in the ocean.
In the UK we use 385 million single-use plastic bottles each day. Most of these are blown up into landfill or are incinerated (burned).
A plastic bag will take up to 20 years to break up in the ocean.

Turtles eat plastic bags thinking they are food.

Every day, 300,000 plastic drinks containers are littered in the UK.
Items that are flushed down the toilet can end up in the ocean. Remember the three Ps! Only Pee, Poo and Paper should ever be flushed down the toilet.

figures.shows: A sample document titled "Opening Discussion" with paragraphs of text, and red leader lines labelled a to d pointing at features of the text layout. Label a points to the first paragraph, b to an indented paragraph, c to a paragraph with wide line spacing, and d to a paragraph indented from the left. Below it are three short blocks of "Aaaa" text lines labelled e (left aligned), f (centred) and g (right aligned). Label h points to a column of numbers 1001.3, 0.6 and 1069.13, with a small vertical line below the column.
labels: A document is a record of an event or someone's thoughts so that the information will not be lost. Usually, a document is written but can also be made with pictures and sounds. It can be written on some physical medium such as paper or parchment or it can exist in electronic form.

There is a vast range of documents, some formal, with set designs and layouts and some informal such as personal letters, notes, emails and texts. These don't have any formal layout and the recipient wouldn't expect one.

Formal documents are expected to have definite structures. A business letter usually has the addresses of the sender and receiver at the top, a formal salutation and signature and name and position of sender at the bottom.

A formal structure also makes documents easier to read and understand. Invoices and receipts vary in their fonts and layout, but they all have lists of items and costs, in columns, with the total at the bottom.

Before printing was invented, people went to experts, called scribes, to create anything from official documents to whole books for them. Scribes had to serve long apprenticeships, learning the required structures of different types of documents. As well as learning to read and write, of course.

The crescent-shaped region in the upper left, between the inscribed circle and the quarter-circle arc, is shaded. No measurements are printed on the figure.
figures.original: The diagram shows a circle inscribed inside a square of side length 10 cm. A quarter circle of radius 10 cm is drawn with the vertex of the square as its centre. Find the shaded area.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A rectangle ABCD with A at top left, B at bottom left, C at bottom right and D at top right. O is on side BC, and BC is drawn with O roughly at its midpoint. Dashed lines join O to A and O to D. A circular arc from A over the top point E to D bulges above side AD. The region bounded by the arc AED, and the dashed lines AO and OD, is shaded. No numerical values are printed on the figure.
figures.original: ABCD is a rectangle with AB = 9 cm and BC = 18 cm. O is the midpoint of BC. OAED is a sector of a circle, centre O. Find a AO b angle AOD, in radians c the area of the shaded region.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A shaded sector of a circle, with the apex at the bottom and the two straight radii going up to a curved arc at the top. The angle at the apex is marked with an arc and labelled 1.1 rad. The bottom straight edge is labelled 4 cm.
figures.original: Find the perimeter of each of these sectors.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A shaded sector of a circle with a small arc drawn near the centre marking the angle, labelled 2 rad. The straight bottom radius is labelled 8 cm. The other radius slopes up to the left and the curved arc is at the outer edge.
figures.original: Find the perimeter of each of these sectors.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A shaded sector of a circle with a large reflex angle at the centre, labelled 4.2 rad, marked by an arc around the centre. One straight edge is horizontal and is labelled 5 cm as the radius. The other straight edge slopes down and to the left from the centre.
figures.original: Find the perimeter of each of these sectors.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A rectangle ABCD with A at top left, D at top right, B at bottom left and C at bottom right. O is on the bottom side BC, between B and C. Dashed lines join O to A and O to D. A curved arc from A to D passes through point E at the top, and the shaded region is the sector OAED, bounded by OA, OD and the arc AED. No lengths are printed on the figure.
figures.original: ABCD is a rectangle with AB = 6 cm and BC = 16 cm. O is the midpoint of BC. OAED is a sector of a circle, centre O. Find

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: Two concentric circles with centre O. Points A and B lie on the larger circle, and the radii OA and OB are each labelled 10 cm. The angle AOB is labelled 2.3 rad, and chord AB is drawn. The segment between the chord and the larger circle's arc AB, at the top, is shaded.
figures.original: Find a the length of arc AB b the length of chord AB c the perimeter of the shaded segment.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A triangle EFG with E at the bottom left, F at the bottom right and G at the top. Sides EG and FG are each labelled 16 cm. Point H lies on EF, and an arc from G to H is drawn, with the region between EG, the arc and EH shaded. The angle at F between FH and FG is labelled 0.85 rad.
figures.original: Triangle EFG is isosceles with EG = FG = 16 cm. GH is an arc of a circle, centre F, with angle HFG = 0.85 radians. Find

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: Triangle EFG has EG and FG both labelled 9 cm, and H lies on the base EF. An arc GH is drawn from G to H, and the region between EG, the arc GH and EH is shaded. The angle at F, between FH and FG, is labelled 0.6 rad.
figures.original: Triangle EFG is isosceles with EG = FG = 9 cm. GH is an arc of a circle, centre F, with angle HFG = 0.6 radians. Find

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A circle with centre O and points A and B on the circle, joined by a chord AB. The radii OA and OB are each labelled 12 cm, and the angle at O between them is labelled θ. The arc AB along the top is labelled 9π cm, and the segment between the chord and the arc is shaded light blue.
figures.original: The diagram shows a circle, centre O, radius 12 cm. Angle AOB = θ radians. Arc AB = 9π cm.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: Two sectors share the centre O. The smaller sector AOD has radius OA = OD, and the larger sector BOC has radius OB = OC. A lies on OB and D lies on OC. The region between the two arcs AD and BC, bounded by the straight segments AB and DC, is shaded light blue. No values are printed on the figure.
figures.original: AOD is a sector of a circle, centre O, radius 4 cm. BOC is a sector of a circle, centre O, radius 10 cm. The shaded region has a perimeter of 18 cm. Find

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A sector AOB of a circle with centre O. Point A is on the horizontal radius OA, which is 9 cm long, and point B is on the arc. Point C lies on OB with OC = 5 cm, and the angle at O between OA and OB is marked 0.5 rad. Point D lies on OA with CD perpendicular to OA, marked by a right-angle symbol. The region bounded by CD, DA, the arc AB and BC is shaded.
figures.original: AOB is a sector of a circle, centre O, with radius 9 cm. Angle COD = 0.5 radians and angle ODC is a right angle. OC = 5 cm. Find

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: Two concentric circular sectors share a centre O. The smaller sector is EOH and the larger is FOG. E and F lie on the straight line from O along the bottom, and H and G lie on the straight line from O going up to the right. The region between the two arcs, bounded by EF, arc FG, GH and arc HE, is shaded light blue. No numerical values are printed on the figure.
figures.original: FOG is a sector of a circle, centre O, with angle FOG = 1.2 radians. EOH is a sector of a circle, centre O, with radius 5 cm. The shaded region has an area of 71.4 cm². Find the perimeter of the shaded region.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: Two overlapping circles of equal radius, with centres A and B, where B lies on the circle centred at A. The circles meet at C (top) and D (bottom). Line AB is extended to E on the circle centred at B, and the distance from B to E is labelled 10 cm. Lines AC, BC, BD, CD (chord) and DE are drawn. The region bounded by the arc CE of circle B, the line segments ED and DB, and the arc BD of circle A is shaded blue (also including the area to the right of arc CB).
figures.original: The diagram shows two circles, centres A and B, each of radius 10cm. The point B lies on the circumference of the circle with centre A. The two circles intersect at the points C and D. The point E lies on the circumference of the circle centre B such that ABE is a diameter.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A circle with centre O and points P and Q on the circle. The radii OP and OQ are drawn, with OP labelled 8 cm and the angle POQ marked as 3/4 rad. Tangents PT and QT meet at an external point T, and the region bounded by PT, QT and the minor arc PQ is shaded light blue.
figures.original: The diagram shows a circle, centre O, radius 8 cm. The points P and Q lie on the circle. The lines PT and QT are tangents to the circle and angle POQ = 3π/4 radians.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A sector OPQ of a circle with centre O, where O, P and Q are labelled. OP is the horizontal radius, marked as x cm, and OQ is the other radius. The angle at O between OP and OQ is 0.8 rad. S is a point on OQ with OS = 5 cm. R is a point on OP such that SR is perpendicular to OP, marked with a right angle. The region bounded by SR, RP, arc PQ and QS is shaded.
figures.original: The diagram shows a sector OPQ of a circle with centre O and radius x cm.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A circle with centre O and a chord AB. Dashed radii OA and OB are drawn from O to points A and B on the circle, and OA is labelled 12 cm. The angle AOB at O is marked with an arc and labelled 1.4 rad. The chord AB is drawn as a solid line.
figures.original: The diagram shows a circle with centre O and a chord AB.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A square ABCD with A at top left, D at top right, B at bottom left and C at bottom right; the side is 16 cm. M is on side AB, at its midpoint. E is on AD with AE = 6 cm, and F is on BC. Straight lines join M to E and M to F, and an arc EF centred at M bulges to the right. The angle EMF is marked θ rad. The region to the right of the arc, between the arc and the sides ED, DC and CF, is shaded blue.
figures.original: The diagram shows a square ABCD of side 16 cm. M is the mid-point of AB. The points E and F are on AD and BC respectively such that AE = BF = 6 cm. EF is an arc of the circle centre M, such that angle EMF is θ radians.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A shaded shape made of a right-angled triangle ABC and a circular sector with centre C. A is at the bottom left with a right-angle mark, B is directly above A, and C lies on the horizontal line AD. The sector's arc runs from B to D, with D on the horizontal line, and CD is marked 12 cm. The angle ACB is marked 1 rad.
figures.original: The diagram shows a right-angled triangle ABC and a sector CBDC of a circle with centre C and radius 12 cm. Angle ACB = 1 radian and ACD is a straight line.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A graph of a tangent-type curve drawn for x from 0 to 2π, with the axes labelled x and y. Vertical dashed asymptotes are drawn at x = π/2 and x = 3π/2, and a horizontal dashed line is drawn at y = 3. The curve starts at (0, 3) and rises steeply toward the asymptote at π/2. It passes through the labelled point P on this first branch. The middle branch crosses the x-axis, passes through (π, 3), and rises toward the asymptote at 3π/2. The last branch rises from below and ends at (2π, 3).
figures.original: Part of the graph of y = A tan Bx + C is shown above. The graph passes through the point P(π/4, 4). Find the value of A, the value of B and the value of C.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A smooth curve is drawn on a grid with x from 0 to π and y from 0 to 7, with the y-axis marked 1 to 7 and the x-axis marked at π/2 and π. The curve starts at y = 2 when x = 0, rises to a maximum of 6 at x = π/2 (marked by a vertical grid line), and falls back to y = 2 at x = π. The curve is symmetric about x = π/2.
figures.original: The graph of y = a + b sin cx, for 0 ≤ x ≤ π, is shown above. Write down the value of a, the value of b and the value of c.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A graph of a sine-type curve on axes with x from 0 to 180 and y from 0 to 8. The curve starts at (0, 4), rises to a maximum of 7 at x = 45, falls through y = 4 at x = 90 to a minimum of 1 at x = 135, and rises back to y = 4 at x = 180. Horizontal gridlines are at each integer y value, and there is a vertical line at x = 90.
figures.original: Part of the graph of y = a sin bx + c is shown above. Write down the value of a, the value of b and the value of c.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A blue sinusoidal curve is drawn on axes x and y from x = 0 to x = 2π, with two full periods. The curve has maximum value 4 and minimum value -2, and starts at about y = 1 at x = 0. It crosses y = 1 at x = π and again at x = 2π. Red dashed horizontal lines mark y = 4, y = 1 and y = -2. Red dashed vertical lines mark x = π and x = 2π.
figures.original: State the value of a, of b and of c.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: Seven hexagons are arranged in a honeycomb, one in the centre and six around it. Each hexagon holds one trigonometric expression. The centre hexagon is blue, and the surrounding ones are coloured grey, orange or blue.
labels: cosec x − cot x cos x
cot x sin x tan x
figures.original: Find the trigonometric expression that does not match the other six expressions.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A blue wave-shaped curve is drawn on axes with x from 0 to 180° and y marked 0 to 12 in steps of 2. The curve has a maximum of 10 and a minimum of 4, marked by red dashed horizontal lines at y = 10 and y = 4. It completes four full cycles between x = 0 and x = 180°, starting at about y = 7.5 on the y-axis. A red dashed vertical line marks x = 180°.
figures.original: The diagram shows a sketch of the curve y = a sin(bx) + c for 0° ≤ x ≤ 180°. Find the values of a, b and c.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A row of nine separate square cards, each printed with one capital letter. Read from left to right, the letters spell G, R, A, D, I, E, N, T, S.
figures.original: a Find the number of different arrangements of these nine cards if there are no restrictions.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A single row of seven shapes. The first four are squares and the last three are circles. Each shape has a pale fill and a coloured outline. In order they are: a blue square, an orange square, a green square, a red square, a blue circle, an orange circle and a green circle.
figures.original: a Find the number of different arrangements of these seven objects if there are no restrictions.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: Two separate drawings of cubes (boxes) drawn in three-dimensional perspective. The box on the left has a letter A on its front face and the box on the right has a letter B on its front face.
figures.original: The diagram shows 2 different boxes, A and B. 8 different toys are to be placed in the boxes. Find the number of ways in which the 8 toys can be placed in the boxes so that 5 toys are in box A and 3 toys are in box B.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A table with two rows. The row 'Number on ball' has the values 0, 1, 2, 3, and the row 'Frequency' has the matching values 2, 6, 5, 7.
figures.original: Four of these balls are chosen at random, without replacement. Calculate the number of ways this can be done so that

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A triangle outline containing the first six rows of Pascal's triangle after the top 1. Row 1: 1, 1. Row 2: 1, 2, 1. Row 3: 1, 3, 3, 1. Row 4: 1, 4, 6, 4, 1. Row 5: 1, 5, 10, 10, 5, 1. Row 6: 1, 6, 15, 20, 15, 6, 1. Most numbers are orange, but the 1 in row 3, the 4 in row 4, the 10 in row 5 and the 20 in row 6 are blue.
figures.original: Which other number patterns can you find in Pascal's triangle?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A 5 by 5 grid of square stepping stones. START is at the top left and FINISH, shaded orange, is at the bottom right. The other stones are labelled by row: B, E, I, N; A, D, H, M, R; C, G, L, Q, U; F, K, P, T, W; J, O, S, V. Three coloured routes (blue, black and orange) run from START to stone G, and a small "3" is printed next to G.
figures.original: The diagram shows there are 3 routes from the START stone to stone G.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A two-column table headed Pattern and Area, with rows for patterns 1 to 4. Each area is a sum of terms of the form (number) × √3(length)²/4. Pattern 1 is √3x²/4. Pattern 2 adds 3 × √3(x/3)²/4. Pattern 3 adds 12 × √3(x/9)²/4 to pattern 2. Pattern 4 adds 48 × √3(x/27)²/4 to pattern 3.
figures.original: b Show that the area of each of patterns 1, 2, 3 and 4 can be written as

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A graph of the curve y = x e^x drawn on x and y axes with the origin labelled O. The curve passes through the origin and rises to the right. The region under the curve between x = 0 and x = 2 is shaded light blue, bounded on the right by a dashed vertical line at x = 2.
figures.original: b Use your result from part a to evaluate the area of the shaded region.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A graph with x- and y-axes meeting at the origin O. A decreasing curve lies in the first quadrant and gets steeper as it nears the y-axis, and it flattens toward the x-axis as x increases. The region under the curve between x = 1 and x = k is shaded, with dashed vertical lines from the curve down to the x-axis at x = 1 and x = k.
figures.original: The diagram shows part of the curve y = 4/(2x − 1). Given that the shaded region has area 8, find the exact value of k.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A graph of the curve y = ln x on x and y axes with origin O. The curve crosses the x-axis at x = 1 and rises to the right. The region under the curve between x = 1 and x = 5 is shaded, with a dashed vertical line at x = 5.
figures.original: b Use your result from part a to evaluate the area of the shaded region.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A graph of the curve y = x² − 3x, drawn as an upward-opening parabola on x and y axes with the origin labelled O. The curve crosses the x-axis at O and at x = 3. The region between the curve and the x-axis, from x = 0 to x = 3, is shaded.
figures.original: Find the area of the shaded region.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A graph of the curve y = x² drawn on x and y axes with origin O, rising from the origin through the first quadrant. The region under the curve between the dashed vertical lines at x = 2 and x = 3 is shaded, bounded below by the x-axis.
figures.original: Find the area of the shaded region.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A curve labelled y = 1 + e^(1/2) (the exponent appears to be x/2, but the image shows it as printed) rises from left to right above the x-axis, with axes labelled x, y and origin O. Dashed vertical lines at x = 1 and x = 3 bound a shaded region between the curve and the x-axis.
figures.original: Find the area of the shaded region.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A graph of the curve y = 2 sin x + 3 cos x, drawn on axes with origin O, x-axis and y-axis labelled. The curve starts at a positive y-intercept, rises to a maximum, then falls. The region under the curve between x = 0 and x = π/2 is shaded, with a dashed vertical line at x = π/2.
figures.original: e y = 2 sin x + 3 cos x

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A curve labelled y = 1 + sin 2x is drawn on x–y axes with origin O. The curve starts above the x-axis on the y-axis, rises to a maximum at x = π/4, then falls. Dashed vertical lines at x = π/4 and x = π/2 mark the edges of a shaded region under the curve between them, down to the x-axis.
figures.original: f y = 1 + sin 2x

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A graph of the parabola y = x(x − 2) on x and y axes with origin O. The curve opens upward and crosses the x-axis at O and at x = 2. The region between the curve and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 2 lies below the axis and is shaded light blue.
figures.original: a y = x(x − 2)

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A graph with x and y axes and origin O shows an increasing curve y = x − 5cos(x/2). The curve starts below the x-axis on the y-axis and crosses the x-axis at a point to the right. Two vertical dashed lines at x = π/3 and x = π/2 bound a shaded region between the curve and the x-axis. The region lies below the x-axis.
figures.original: b y = x − 5 cos(x/2)

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A graph with x and y axes and origin O, showing the decreasing curve y = 4/(x + 2), which starts at a positive y-intercept and levels off as x increases. The region under the curve between the y-axis (x = 0) and a dashed vertical line at x = 3 is shaded light blue.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A curve y = x + 2/(2x + 3) is drawn on x–y axes. It falls from the top left to a minimum a little to the left of the y-axis, then rises to the right. The region under the curve between x = -1 and x = 1 is shaded light blue, with dashed vertical lines at x = -1 and x = 1.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A graph with x and y axes and origin O shows a bell-shaped cosine curve labelled y = 1 + cos x. A horizontal line labelled y = 1 crosses the curve at two points. The region between the curve and the line, above the line, is shaded light blue.
figures.original: Find the area of the region enclosed by the curve y = 1 + cos x and the line y = 1.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A downward-opening parabola labelled y = 2 + 3x − x² is drawn on x and y axes with origin O. The curve crosses the y-axis at 2, and a dashed horizontal line runs from y = 2 across to x = 2. A dashed vertical line runs from x = 2 on the x-axis up to the curve. The region between the curve, the y-axis, the line y = 2 and the line x = 2 is shaded blue.
figures.original: Find the area of the region bounded by the curve y = 2 + 3x − x², the line x = 2 and the line y = 2.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A graph with x and y axes meeting at the origin O. A curve labelled y = 3x² + 2 is drawn, starting on the y-axis above O and rising to the right. A dashed horizontal line at y = 14 meets the curve, and the region between the curve, the y-axis and the dashed line is shaded light blue.
figures.original: Find the area of the region bounded by the curve y = 3x² + 2, the line y = 14 and the y-axis.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A curve labelled y = 2 sin 2x + 3 cos x starts on the y-axis at the point 3. It rises to a maximum and then falls to meet the x-axis at x = π/2. A straight line runs from (0, 3) down to (π/2, 0). The region between the curve and the line is shaded.
figures.original: Find the area of the shaded region.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A graph with x- and y-axes meeting at the origin O. It shows the curve y = 3√x and the straight line y = 10 − x, which cross in the first quadrant. The region under the curve and the line, above the x-axis and to the right of the y-axis, is shaded light blue. The line meets the y-axis at the top left and the x-axis on the right.
figures.original: Find the shaded area enclosed by the curve y = 3√x the line y = 10 − x and the x-axis.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A downward-opening parabola y = 6x − x² crossing the x-axis at the origin O and at x = 6, with its peak between them. A straight tangent line touches the curve at the point labelled (2, 8) and cuts the negative x-axis at a point labelled P. The region bounded by the tangent line, the curve and the x-axis is shaded.
figures.original: The tangent to the curve y = 6x − x² at the point (2, 8) cuts the x-axis at the point P. a Find the coordinates of P. b Find the area of the shaded region.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A set of axes with x and y labelled and origin O, showing the curve y = √(2x+1) rising from the y-axis. The point P is on the y-axis where the curve starts, and the point R is higher on the y-axis. A straight tangent line from R touches the curve at the point Q(12, 5), and the thin region between the curve, the tangent and the y-axis is shaded.
figures.original: The curve y = √(2x+1) meets the y-axis at the point P. The tangent at the point Q(12, 5) to this curve meets the y-axis at the point R. Find the area of the shaded region PQR.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: Two curves are drawn on x–y axes from x = 0 to x = π, with the origin labelled O. The upper curve is labelled y = 2 + cos 2x and the lower curve is labelled y = 1 + 2 cos 2x. They meet at x = 0 and at x = π, which is marked with a dashed vertical line. The region between them is shaded, and the lower curve dips below the x-axis.
figures.original: The diagram shows the graphs of y = 2 + cos 2x and y = 1 + 2 cos 2x for 0 ≤ x ≤ π. Find the area of the shaded region.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A graph with x- and y-axes (origin O) showing the decreasing straight line y = 4 − x and the curve y = 6/(x+3). The line and curve intersect at two points, one in the upper left and one in the lower right. The region between them is shaded. The curve lies below the line in the shaded region and crosses the y-axis below the line.
figures.original: The diagram shows the graphs of y = 6/(x+3) and y = 4 − x. Find the area of the shaded region.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A graph of the curve y = x sin x, labelled on the figure, drawn for x from 0 to π. The curve starts at the origin O, rises to a maximum between π/2 and π, then falls to meet the x-axis at π. A dashed vertical line runs from the curve at x = π/2 down to the x-axis. The region under the curve between x = π/2 and x = π is shaded.
figures.original: b Use your result from part a to evaluate the area of the shaded region.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE® and O Level Additional Mathematics Coursebook (Sue Pemberton)
figures.shows: A set of axes with origin O and the x-axis marked at 8. A downward-opening parabola y = x(8 − x) and a straight line y = 3x both pass through the origin, and the line crosses the curve near the top right of the curve. favourable movement of Na+ drives the uptake of glucose against its concentration gradient.

Figure 1.07 shows the sampling operation of the ADC. The amplitude of the wave (the red line) has to
be sampled at regular intervals. The blue vertical lines indicate the sampling times. The amplitude
cannot be measured exactly; instead the amplitude is approximated by the closest of the defined
amplitudes represented by the horizontal lines. In Figure 1.07, sample values 1 and 4 will be an
accurate estimate of the actual amplitude because the wave is touching an amplitude line. In contrast,
samples 5 and 6 will not be accurate because the actual amplitude is approximately half way between
the two closest defined values.

Pre-condition loops
Pre-condition loops, as the name suggests, evaluate the condition before the statements within the loop
are executed. Pre-condition loops will execute the statements within the loop as long as the condition
evaluates to True. When the condition evaluates to False, execution will go to the next statement after
the loop.
